Comment: Fungal data: The Euk primers are good for a lot of eukaryotic organisms, so it seems
like one stone for many birds. However, for fungi, it provides very poor resolution and this
becomes an even bigger problem since the typical amplicon size derived from these primers is
really short (~180 bp). Furthermore, the threshold for rarefying fungal data is also too low. I

rarefaction plots should be provided for both bacteria and fungi.
Answer: We thank the reviewer for these insightful comments. We acknowledge that universal
eukaryotic primers targeting the 18S rRNA region have lower taxonomic resolution for fungi
compared with ITS markers. However, 18S-based amplicons remain widely used in large-scale
fungal ecology and biogeography studies16, particularly when the goal is to quantify broad-
scale diversity patterns rather than species-level taxonomy. Importantly, our dataset yielded
more than 6,000 high-quality fungal ASVs across global biomes, a richness level comparable
to (or exceeding) those reported in ITS amplicon surveys17-19. This demonstrates that, despite
the inherent limitations, the 18S dataset in this study provides robust and representative fungal
diversity patterns suitable for the large-scale comparative analyses.
To assess the adequacy of sequencing depth, we have now included rarefaction curves for both
bacterial and fungal datasets (Extended Data Fig. S10 and see figure below). For fungal data,
we additionally increased the rarefaction depth from 2,000 to 4,000 reads per sample and found
that diversity estimates (e.g., Shannon index) were highly correlated (r = 0.99) between the two
depths (see figures below), indicating that our results are robust to sequencing depth. We
therefore believe that, despite the inherent limitations of short-read 18S data, the fungal dataset
provides reliable comparative diversity patterns suitable for large-scale cross-biome analyses.

Comment: Greenhouse study: I appreciate that the authors attempted to validate their diversity-
pathogen relationship, but there are important issues. First of all, it is not clear if this
greenhouse study was conducted in the presence of a host plant or not. If not, why do it in the
greenhouse? Secondly, the authors used OD600 and inoculated a 15 mL suspension. OD600 is
a crude measure and can be affected by dead cells and different sizes, especially in this case.
Cell count using Flow Cytometry would have been better. More importantly, 15 mL reads
arbitrary- why 15 and not 10 or 20? Was it adequate for a 3 L pot? Did you just add it on top
of the pots or a few mm into the soil? When you collected samples, did you collect from the
topsoil, especially since the pot size was 3 L. Also, how much soil sample was collected at each
time point? Important details are missing. Lastly, the validation only involved two pathogens-
Streptomyces scabiei and Ralstonia solanacearum, so the findings must be interpreted with
caution.
Answer: We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments.
The experiment was performed without host plants, because the aim of this validation was to
provide a controlled microcosm system to test whether the negative relationship between soil
microbial diversity and pathogen abundance observed in the global dataset is also detectable
under standardized experimental condition, independent of plant-mediated immunity or
rhizosphere effects. We have now revised the text to make this clear in lines 954-956 ‘All
experimental units were maintained in controlled greenhouse conditions (without host plants)
with standardized irrigation protocols.’.
We agree that OD600 is a relatively coarse estimate of cell density. However, it is routinely
used in soil inoculation experiments and provides sufficient reproducibility when the same
growth phase and optical calibration are used20-22. To ensure the accuracy and consistency of
our inoculum, we standardized the bacterial suspensions to a target OD600 and then estimated
the corresponding CFU/mL values. For the inoculation volume (15 mL), actually we added 1.5
kg soil to a 3 L pot, so the 15 mL suspension is for 1.5 kg soil. This dosage estimated around
1×10⁶ CFU per gram of soil, which falls within the well-established range used in soil pathogen
introduction assays23. We have clarified this in lines 952-954 ‘The applied inoculum
corresponded to an estimated initial concentration of ~10⁶ CFU per gram of soil, which lies
within the commonly used range for soil-borne pathogen introduction assays in controlled
experiments88.’.
At each time point, around 5 g of soil was collected from the top 0–5 cm layer using sterile
corers, pooled from three subsites within the same pot to reduce spatial heterogeneity. These
details have been added to the revised text in lines 957-959 ‘At each time point, around 5 g of
soil was collected from the top 0–5 cm layer using sterile corers, pooled from three subsites
within the same pot to reduce spatial heterogeneity.’.
For the validation work, we chose Ralstonia solanacearum and Streptomyces scabiei because
they are among the most dominant pathogens, differ strongly in phylogeny (Gram-negative vs.
Gram-positive) and Mean Annual Precipitation (MAP) preference (MAP- negative vs. MAP-
positive), allowing us to test whether the diversity–suppression pattern generalizes across
contrasting pathogen types irrespective of microbial traits and environmental preference. We
now clearly describe the choice of these organisms in lines 272-280 ‘For this validation
experiment, we selected two model and dominant pathogens, which have differential mode of
infection and environmental preferences—S. scabiei (a necrotrophic pathogen favouring drier
soils)21 and R. solanacearum (a vascular wilt pathogen thriving in moist environments)20—
allowing us to test whether the diversity–suppression pattern generalizes across contrasting
pathogen types irrespective of microbial traits and environmental preference. Although our
findings are supported by plot/ pot scale studies for other pathogens41,47, future studies should
incorporate a broader spectrum of pathogens to generalize the diversity-pathogen inhibition
relationship observed in this study.’.

‘randomForest’99 and ‘rfPermute’ package100 in R to explore the ecological factors (such as

Comment: Dominant pathogen: I find their threshold for defining a dominant pathogen too
stringent. Prevalence of 100% of samples and relative abundance in the top 30% can bias the
dataset towards only ubiquity and ignore locally devastating pathogens. Basically, relative
abundance and presence (ubiquity) do not necessarily correspond to virulence potential.
Answer: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We agree that a 100% prevalence threshold
would be overly stringent and could bias the analysis toward ubiquitous taxa. We clarify that
dominant pathogens were defined using a prevalence threshold of > 80%, and the 100%
prevalence in the manuscript was a textual error that has now been corrected. The 80%
threshold was chosen to identify globally dominant pathogens, and lowering this threshold
yielded consistent results (Supplementary Dataset). We have correlated sentence in lines 830-
833 read as ‘In total, we identified 107 bacterial pathogen species, of which 32 were classified
as globally dominant based on their high frequency of occurrence (present in at least 80% of
samples) and high relative abundance (top 30%, with a mean relative abundance ≥ 0.1%)
across global soils (Fig. 1).’.
We agree that global prevalence does not equate to virulence, and that locally devastating
pathogens may be missed by a frequency-based definition. Indeed, we did explore the
correlation between pathogens abundance and validated virulence genes curated in the
Pathogen–Host Interaction database (PHI-base), and a lot of pathogen species demonstrate
positive correlation (Extended Data Fig. S8). However, the main objective of this study was to
characterize globally dominant pathogens, their drivers and distributions and abundance
patterns; detailed assessments of virulence traits and epidemic severity are beyond the scope
of our manuscript but represent an important direction for future research. We have included a
clarification in line 371-373 ‘While this study focuses on pathogen dominance and suppression,
predicting pathogen virulence and disease severity associated with dominance represents an
important next research direction.’
Comment: The relationship between microbial diversity and pathogen is not really strong.
Sometimes it was even less than 0.01. I wouldn’t call it ‘robust’. Exercise caution while
interpreting.
Answer: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We agree that the correlation between
microbial diversity (based on Kraken2 metagenomic estimates) and pathogen abundance is not
numerically strong (r = –0.051, P = 0.039; n = 1,602), although statistically significant. Effect
sizes in the range of r = 0.05~0.20 have also been reported in other global soil microbiome
studies24,25, and are considered ecologically meaningful when the direction of association is
consistent across spatial scales. Moreover, pathogen abundance is shaped by a suite of
interacting abiotic and biotic factors, and shotgun metagenomic meta-analyses inherently carry
substantial biological and technical noise, which typically reduces effect sizes. Importantly,
when microbial diversity was derived from our standardized amplicon dataset, the negative
association strengthened (r = –0.22, P = 0.003). This pattern was further supported by our
independent greenhouse experiment. Collectively, these results indicate a modest but
statistically supported negative relationship between microbial diversity and pathogen
abundance. We have included a clarification in lines 260-266 ‘Microbial taxonomic diversity
estimated by Kraken2 and KEGG functional diversity both exhibited modest yet statistically
significant negative correlations with the total relative abundance of dominant bacterial plant
pathogens (Kraken2: rho = −0.051, P = 0.039; KEGG: rho = −0.13, P = 2.44 × 10⁻⁷; n = 1,602;
Fig. 3a). Analyses of bacterial and fungal diversity indices from amplicon sequencing data
showed a strong and significant negative correlation with total relative abundance of bacterial
plant pathogens (bacteria: rho = -0.20, P = 0.006; fungi: rho = -0.18, P = 0.013; n = 200) (Fig.
3b).’, and in lines 270-272 ‘Our data demonstrate a clear link between higher microbial
diversity and the early suppression of pathogen invasion, with more diverse soils reducing the
absolute abundances of both pathogens as quantified by qPCR (Fig. 3c).’.
Comment: While climatic factors are certainly important for pathogen prevalence, as shown in
this study, management and agronomic factors are also critical. For example, the application of
fungicides or pesticides, adoption of resistant varieties and crop rotation, etc. can determine
pathogen outbreaks and prevalence at a local scale, potentially impacting global scale
projections done in this study. I would be careful in interpretations and conclusions and not
attribute everything to climate change.
Answer: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We fully agree that agronomic practices—
such as pesticide application, crop rotation, and the use of resistant cultivars—can influence

drivers of pathogen distributions and suppression are affected by regional and local conditions
including management practices (e.g., use of resistant varieties, antibiotics, and crop-rotations).
There, we have clarified this in the manuscript, lines 368-371 ‘Future work should assess how
the global drivers of pathogen prevalence and suppression identified here interact with local

Answer: Thank you for this comment. We appreciate the concern regarding the amount of

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript entitled “Dominance and natural suppression of bacterial plant pathogens
across global soils” by Gao et al., identified 32 dominant bacterial plant pathogens, their
genomic traits, and evidence of natural soil suppression, by combining a global survey and
public databases, including 1,602 soil metagenomes and an independent greenhouse
experiment. The authors found that pathogen suppression was strongest in global cold-climate
hot-spots, driven by high soil organic carbon, microbial diversity, and abundance; non-
pathogenic Streptomyces, mycorrhizal fungi, lichenized fungi, and terpene/polyketide gene
clusters all negatively correlated with pathogen prevalence; and that future climates are
projected to increase many pathogens, particularly in tropical Africa, North America, and
Eurasia. This study establishes a foundational atlas of soil-borne plant pathogens, advancing
ecological knowledge and guiding future surveillance and management to protect food security
and sustainability. Overall, the research topic is very interesting and important, but I have
several critical comments.
Answer: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive and encouraging assessment of our
work. We appreciate the recognition of our study’s novelty, global scope, and contribution to
understanding the ecological drivers of soil-borne bacterial plant pathogens and natural soil
suppression. We have carefully addressed all of the reviewer’s comments by adding new
analyses, clarifying methodological details, and improving the overall clarity and precision of
the manuscript. All revisions are detailed in the point-by-point responses below.
Major comments:
1: The dilution-to-extinction approach presents a potential confounding factor, as it might
inadvertently introduce bacterial pathogens. The manuscript should address the extent of this
potential influence. Furthermore, the experimental design requires clarification regarding the
controls used—for instance, whether a set of dilutions was maintained without pathogen
inoculation to account for background effects. Additionally, it is crucial to justify whether the
chosen sampling period (3 to 21 days post-inoculation) was sufficient for the microbial
community to stabilize.
Answer: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We acknowledge that soil dilution
may theoretically introduce low-abundance background pathogens. To minimize this
possibility, we: (i) collected the source soil from an untreated natural site with no known history
of plant disease; (ii) prepared all dilution treatments from the same initial soil, ensuring that
any background pathogen load was consistent across treatments; and (iii) included a pathogen-
free control (dilution-only, no inoculation) and measure the pathogen background levels across
treatments. We have now included a new Extended figure (Extended Data Fig. S11) to show
the qPCR quantification of S. scabiei and R. solanacearum in the dilution controls prior to
pathogen inoculation, confirming negligible background levels across treatments (the
abundance of background pathogens in the soil was less than 0.01% of the abundance of the
inoculated pathogens, figure shows below). These results indicate that background pathogen
levels are minimal and would not bias the experimental outcomes or confound the
interpretation of the inoculated pathogen dynamics.
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the 21-day duration of our greenhouse
experiment. Prior to pathogen inoculation, soils were incubated for six months to allow
microbial communities to establish and stabilize, and for microbial biomass to recover
following inoculation at different levels of microbial diversity. Following pathogen inoculation,
the short-term monitoring period was intentionally chosen to capture the initial establishment
of the pathogens and the early suppressive responses of the soil microbiome. While longer-
term monitoring would indeed be valuable to assess the temporal stability of this effect and
represents an important direction for future research, the current timeframe was appropriate to
test for the presence of a diversity-mediated suppression effects. To clarify the scope of our
study, we have revised the manuscript in lines 941-942 ‘The inoculated soils were incubated
at room temperature for six months to facilitate microbial community assembly and
stabilization.’, and in lines 266-269 ‘To experimentally validate these patterns, we manipulated
soil microbial diversity using a dilution-to-extinction approach50, incubated the inoculated soils
for six months, and subsequently introduced pathogens for short-term monitoring.’. We also
added further clarifications in lines 270-272 ‘Our data demonstrate a clear link between higher
microbial diversity and the early suppression of pathogen invasion, with more diverse soils
reducing the absolute abundances of both pathogens as quantified by qPCR (Fig. 3c).’.

The authors have made a reasonable effort to address my previous comments, and the manuscript has improved since the initial submission. However, a few issues still remain that should be addressed before publication. These are mainly related to interpretations rather than data quality or analytical approaches.
In several places, statistically significant but relatively small effect sizes are described using language that implies strong or ‘robust’ relationships. Given the scale of the analysis and the inherent noise in global metagenomic datasets, I think the authors should describe these associations as consistent or supported rather than strong. They can tone down the claims and conclusions, particularly in the abstract, results and conclusions.
Secondly, the manuscript sometimes moves too quickly from correlations to implied mechanisms. For example, while the greenhouse experiment provides decent support for the diversity-pathogen relationship, its scope is limited to two pathogens (which they mentioned) and early invasion dynamics, and more importantly, in the absence of host plants. This kind of pitching overstates their current practical or diagnostic value, as the authors did not evaluate any thresholds or predictive performances. Referring to these features as candidate or putative indicators would be better.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Soils are the primary environmental reservoir of plant pathogens impacting food production and
ecosystem productivity worldwide. Yet, some soils can also suppress pathogens through
environmental and microbial regulation. Here we integrate 1,602 soil metagenomes from 59
countries with a greenhouse experiment to identify 32 dominant pathogens, including Ralstonia
solanacearum, Clavibacter michiganensis, and Streptomyces europaeiscabiei. Pathogen hotspots
occur primarily in warm ecosystems and agricultural soils, whereas higher soil microbial diversity,
increased soil organic carbon and colder climatic conditions are associated with lower pathogen
prevalence. Non-pathogenic Streptomyces spp., arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, and biosynthetic
gene clusters encoding terpenes and polyketides are associated with reduced pathogen prevalence.
Predictive modelling suggests that several dominant bacterial pathogens are likely to increase in
prevalence under future climate scenarios, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. By
identifying global drivers of dominant pathogens and their suppression, this study provides a
foundation for improved surveillance and management of plant disease risks under climate change.

---

## Introduction

Plant diseases caused by bacterial pathogens substantially reduce global primary productivity and
threaten food security1-3. In agricultural systems, they directly undermine crop yields, while in
natural ecosystems their increased prevalence can lower primary productivity, diminishing
biodiversity and ecosystem carbon storage4. Although soils are the largest reservoir of plant
pathogens, they also possess an inherent capacity to suppress pathogen abundance and disease
outbreaks5. Understanding how bacterial pathogens are distributed across soils, and how they
interact with co-existing microbial communities, is therefore essential for identifying the
environmental and biological conditions that promote or limit their prevalence.

Despite evidence that soils play a central role in regulating the survival, proliferation, and
suppression of plant pathogens, major knowledge gaps persist regarding the ecology of soil-borne
bacterial plant pathogens. Three factors largely explain this deficiency. First, most previous
research has focused on fungal and oomycetes pathogens6-8, while bacterial plant pathogens have
received comparatively less attention, in part because conventional markers such as 16S rRNA
genes have limited power to distinguish pathogenic from non-pathogenic species. Second, we
currently lack a comprehensive, standardized assessment of the global biogeography and
environmental controls of bacterial pathogens in soils. Unlike fungal and oomycete taxa, whose
global distributions are known to be strongly shaped by temperature and precipitation6, comparable
insights for bacterial plant pathogens remain unresolved owing to limited taxonomic resolution
and the absence of global-scale metagenomic datasets. Finally, although some soils naturally
suppress pathogen abundance and infection, the specific biological and environmental
determinants of this suppression remain poorly defined across global ecosystems. In particular, the
roles of microbial diversity, functional traits, and competing microbial taxa in constraining
bacterial pathogens in soils have not been quantified at a global scale. Together, these gaps
severely limit our ability to anticipate pathogen emergence, identify soils with inherent suppressive
properties, and develop targeted strategies to monitor and mitigate plant disease risks under rapid
environmental change. Given that plant diseases already impose multibillion-dollar annual losses9-
11 and threaten global food security2,12-15, resolving these fundamental unknowns is urgently
needed to inform future surveillance, management, and policy interventions.

To address existing knowledge gaps, we combined data from public databases (1,402 samples)
with a standardized global field survey (200 samples)16, together comprising 1,602 soil
metagenomes from 59 countries (Supplementary Figure 1 and Supplementary Data 1), to: (1)
determine the global distribution of dominant soil-borne bacterial plant pathogens; (2) identify the
environmental conditions, soil microbial diversity, and microbial and metabolic traits associated
with pathogen-suppressive soils; and (3) predict the current and future global distributions of these
dominant bacterial plant pathogens. To achieve this, we integrated metagenomic and pathogen
genomic analyses with amplicon sequencing and qPCR data from a global field survey, together
with machine-learning and predictive modelling approaches. To further validate the microbial
diversity–suppression relationship identified in the global dataset, we conducted a controlled
greenhouse experiment to directly test the effects of soil biodiversity on pathogen suppression.
Emerging global evidence suggests that higher microbiome diversity can constrain human and
animal pathogens (identified based on 16s rRNA genes) in the plant rhizosphere17. Thus, we
predict that soil biodiversity similarly functions as a key biotic barrier that suppresses soil-borne
bacterial plant pathogens by outcompeting pathogens in the soil. We also expect that warmer and
drier climates, and lower soil organic carbon (OC) would be associated with a higher prevalence
of soil-borne bacterial plant pathogens6,7,18. Our overarching aim was to identify globally dominant
soil-borne bacterial plant pathogens, characterize their distribution and ecological drivers, and
determine the environmental and biological factors that promote natural pathogen suppression.

---

## Results

Dominant bacterial plant pathogens across global soils
First, we constructed a comprehensive bacterial plant pathogen database comprising 310 pathogen
genomes and identified their abundance across global soils using a global soil metagenome dataset.
107 distinct taxa were identified as potential plant pathogens, among which 32 species emerged as
dominant pathogens based on their frequency (detected in 80% of samples) and relative abundance
(top 30%, with average relative abundance ≥ 0.1%) (Fig. 1). These dominant pathogens included
several species from the genera Streptomyces, Rhodococcus, Agrobacterium, Clavibacter,
Ralstonia, Burkholderia, Paracidovorax, Pseudomonas, and Xanthomonas, all known to cause
diseases in a broad range of plants across diverse ecosystems. For example, Ralstonia
solanacearum, the causative agent of bacterial wilt, ranks as the second most destructive bacterial
pathogen globally due to its extensive strain diversity, broad host range, and deleterious impact on
plant productivity19,20. Notably, we identified four Streptomyces species (i.e., S. europaeiscabiei,
S. acidiscabies, S. turgidiscabies, S. scabiei), ranked highly among the dominant pathogens (Fig.
1a and c). This lineage is prominently linked to potato common scab disease21. The adaptability of
these Streptomyces spp. to various environments, particularly their ability to persist as spores in
soil for extended periods and their substantial dispersal abilities, likely contributes to their
dominance21,22.

Comparative genomic analyses further revealed that dominant pathogen species were enriched in
genes associated with signalling and cellular processes, particularly those involved in sugar
transport systems, energy metabolism and carbohydrate metabolism, relative to non-dominant
species (Supplementary Figure 2; Supplementary Table 1). These genes are integral to cellular
communication and function, regulate cell growth and interactions, all of which are critical to
ecological adaptability23,24. Moreover, these genomic signatures support that the pathogenicity
involves signalling mechanisms and ability to penetrate cell wall and membranes25 and underscore
the key genomic adjustments that underpin their prevalence in soil environments.

We next investigated the correlation between the prevalence of key pathogens identified in our
database and independent global observation resources. Our correlation analysis revealed a
positive association between the relative abundance of R. solanacearum (rho = 0.44, P = 0.02, 28
countries) in our dataset and independent observation resource of this pathogen26 (Fig. 2b).
Similarly, the relative abundance of Clavibacter michiganensis (rho = 0.42, P = 0.0047), Robbsia
andropogonis (rho = 0.61, P = 0.0058), and Xanthomonas translucens (rho = 0.53, P = 0.0066)
were positively correlated with their recorded observation in various countries by the EPPO Global
Database (https://gd.eppo.int)27 (Fig. 2b). These country-level correlations demonstrate that the
 that the
relative abundance patterns inferred from our metagenomic database are consistent with
independent global surveillance records, supporting the reliability of our pathogen prevalence
estimates. If these findings are further confirmed at local and regional scales by real farm data, our
framework could support the development of more effective disease surveillance systems,
enabling timely and targeted management and prevention strategies. Taken together, our work
provides insights on the globally dominant bacterial plant pathogens and advances our
understanding of their distribution.

Hotspots of soil bacterial plant pathogens
Next, we sought to understand the conditions that promote the global distribution of bacterial plant
pathogens. Their relative abundance showed distinct patterns across terrestrial soil biomes, with
significantly higher relative abundance observed in farmland compared to other land-use types
(Fig. 2a). This suggests that soils influenced by farm management practices (e.g., monoculture and
use of agrochemicals) may support higher pathogen abundance than natural soils28. In particularly,
pathogens from the genus Pseudomonas, including P. corrugata, P. fuscovaginae, P. marginalis,
P. mediterranea, and P. palleroniana, as well as Pectobacterium carotovorum, were notably more
abundant in farmlands (over 50%, Fig. 1b). These findings highlight the potential role of
agricultural management in shaping the prevalence and distribution of bacterial pathogens.

Random forest analyses identified mean annual temperature (MAT) as a significant factor
affecting the relative abundance of most dominant pathogens (29 out of 32) (Fig. 1c). The influence
of MAT varied among pathogens but generally showed a positive effect on their total abundance
(Fig. 1c, Fig. 2c), suggesting that rising temperatures may exacerbate prevalence of majority of
pathogens6,29,30. This increased prevalence is likely promoted by temperature-induced shortened
incubation periods of pathogens and extended growing seasons of hosts3. The influence of mean
annual precipitation (MAP) varied across pathogen taxa. For example, Streptomyces spp. and
Clavibacter michiganensis showed negative correlations with MAP (Fig. 1c and Supplementary
Figure 3), whereas Rhizobium rhizogenes, Burkholderia spp., Ralstonia solanacearum species
complex, and Xanthomonas spp. exhibited positive correlations with MAP (Fig. 1c and
Supplementary Figure 3). These patterns suggest niche partitioning among pathogens based on
water availability and specific ecological preferences31-36. Taking together, we showed that warmer
ecosystems and farmlands support the largest soil bacterial plant pathogen prevalence worldwide.

The ecology of soil pathogen suppression
We evaluated which set of soil properties and environmental conditions associated with the lowest
prevalence of pathogens, reflecting natural soil pathogen suppression. Correlation analyses
showed that cold ecosystems, as well as soils with higher organic carbon (OC) content, finer soil
textures, and greater microbial diversity, consistently exhibited lower relative abundances of
pathogens (Fig. 1c). To further elucidate the ecological pathways driving these patterns, we
conducted structural equation modelling (SEM) using available metadata. SEM analyses indicated
that MAP exerts direct positive effects on vegetation (measured by NDVI), which in turn enhances
microbial diversity and, ultimately, lower pathogen relative abundance (Fig. 2c). Consistent results
from both correlation and SEM analyses showed that regions characterized by higher microbial
diversity, colder climates, finer soil textures, and elevated soil OC content tend to exhibit lower
pathogen prevalence at the global scale (Fig. 1 and 2). These findings align with research
conducted at plot and farm scales37-41. For example, increasing soil OC, such as through organic
amendments, has been reported to reduce soil-borne diseases by stimulating microbial activity42.
However, the relationship between soil OC and pathogen abundance is complex and varies among
different pathogens and regions. Some studies have reported that increased OC may also lead to
an increase the prevalence of certain fungal pathogens43. This divergence is likely linked to nutrient
preference for soil borne bacterial and fungal/ oomycetes pathogens44, reflecting the distinct
environmental preferences of various pathogens. Overall, our study shows that microbial diversity
and specific soil properties are associated with lower abundances of bacterial plant pathogens
across terrestrial ecosystems.

To further support the observed relationship between soil microbial diversity and pathogen
suppression, we quantified microbial diversity using both shotgun metagenomic and amplicon
sequencing data and conducted a greenhouse experiment in which soil microbial diversity was
experimentally manipulated. We first assessed the microbial taxa diversity (based on the Kraken
2 database)45 and functional diversity (based on KEGG database)46 from 1,602 metagenomic data
and explored their association with the relative abundance of bacterial plant pathogens (Fig. 1 and
Fig. 3a). For the 200 globally standardized field samples, we quantified bacterial abundance using
16S qPCR and characterized bacterial and fungal community diversity through amplicon
sequencing, further exploring their relationships with pathogens. Microbial taxonomic diversity
estimated by Kraken2 and KEGG functional diversity both exhibited modest yet statistically
significant negative correlations with the total relative abundance of dominant bacterial plant
pathogens (Kraken2: rho = −0.051, P = 0.039; KEGG: rho = −0.13, P = 2.44 × 10⁻⁷; n = 1,602;
Fig. 3a). Analyses of bacterial and fungal diversity indices from amplicon sequencing data also
showed a significant negative correlation with total relative abundance of bacterial plant pathogens
(bacteria: rho = -0.20, P = 0.006; fungi: rho = -0.18, P = 0.013; n = 200) (Fig. 3b). To
experimentally validate these patterns, we manipulated soil microbial diversity using a dilution-
to-extinction approach47, incubated the inoculated soils for six months, and subsequently
introduced pathogens for short-term monitoring. For this validation experiment, we selected two
model and dominant pathogens, which have differential mode of infection and environmental
preferences, S. scabiei (a necrotrophic pathogen favouring drier soils)21 and R. solanacearum (a
vascular wilt pathogen thriving in moist environments)20, allowing us to assess whether the
observed diversity–pathogen relationship is consistent across two contrasting and ecologically
distinct model pathogens during early invasion stages. Pathogen abundance was quantified by
qPCR and decreased with increasing soil microbial diversity (Fig. 3c), providing experimental
support for a negative association between microbial diversity and early pathogen invasion
dynamics. Although similar diversity–pathogen patterns have been reported in plot- and pot-scale
studies for other pathogens41,47, future studies incorporating a broader range of pathogen taxa will
be required to assess the generality of this relationship. Additionally, we observed a significantly
negative correlation between soil total bacterial abundance (measured by 16S qPCR) and the
relative abundance of bacterial plant pathogens (rho = -0.30, P = 2.529e-05) in our standardised
global survey study (Fig. 3d), consistently supporting the notion that increased microbial diversity
and bacterial abundance correlates with reduced pathogen load and disease incidence48. Soils with
high microbial diversity and biomass are likely to facilitate complex interactions among coexisting
microbes, encompassing competition, predation, symbiosis, and parasitism48-50, at the expense of
pathogen dominance. Collectively, our results provide global-scale evidence, supported by a
greenhouse validation experiment, that higher soil microbial diversity and bacterial abundance are
associated with reduced abundance of bacterial plant pathogens. These insights reinforce the
importance of agricultural and land-management practices that enhance soil microbial diversity
and biomass to maintain ecosystem services including the defence against plant pathogens51-53.

Microbial taxa and potential metabolic traits linked to soil pathogen suppression
Given the importance of soil microbial diversity in shaping patterns of pathogen prevalence, we
further examined specific microbial taxa within soil microbiomes that are associated with lower
pathogen abundance. Correlation analyses involving 9,619 bacterial taxa identified using the
Kraken 2 database revealed 526 taxa that were negatively correlated with the total relative
abundance of dominant pathogens (using rho < -0.2 and p < 0.0001 as thresholds). Taxa belonging
to the phyla Actinomycetota and Bacillota were predominant among these negatively correlated
groups, accounting for 34.6% and 16.5% of all negatively correlated taxa, respectively. In
particular, the relative abundance of non-pathogenic Streptomyces spp. was negatively associated
with pathogen abundance (rho = -0.08, p = 0.00195) (Fig. 3e), consistent with their known capacity
to produce a wide array of antibiotics and secondary metabolites that inhibit plant pathogens54.
Beyond bacterial communities, we also identified several fungal functional groups that were
negatively associated with pathogen prevalence, including Arbuscular Mycorrhizal fungi (rho = -
0.17, p = 0.017) and lichenized fungi (rho = -0.17, p = 0.017) (Fig. 3f). These fungal groups were
also linked to significant increases in soil bacterial and fungal diversity and abundance
(Supplementary Figure 4), suggesting their potential contribution to pathogen-suppressive soil
contexts across terrestrial ecosystems. Overall, these findings highlight the multifaceted microbial
features associated with lower pathogen abundance in soils across broad ecological contexts,
involving both bacterial antagonists and beneficial fungal symbionts.

To further support our findings, we examined the potential microbial metabolites traits associated
with pathogen-suppressive soils. Metagenomic data were annotated using the antiSMASH
database55 to assess correlations between biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) encoding microbial
metabolites and pathogen abundance. We found that gene clusters encoding terpene (rho = -0.11,
p = 6.063e-06), and type III polyketide synthases (T3PKS; rho = -0.10, p = 2.494e-05) showed the
strongest negative associations with pathogen abundance (Fig3. g). Terpenes, the largest class of
natural products56, are produced by diverse bacteria and fungi, particularly members of the
Streptomycetaceae, and are well documented for their antimicrobial activity57, including effects
on cellular respiration58 and membrane integrity57. Polyketides, another diverse class of natural
products with antimicrobial properties, similarly showed significantly negative associations with
pathogen abundance in our dataset (p < 0.05) and have been widely reported to contribute to
disease suppression by microbes such as Bacillus spp.59, Paenibacillus spp.60, Trichoderma spp.61,
and Flavobacterium spp.5. In addition to terpenes and T3PKS, gene clusters encoding indole,
ranthipeptides, and NRPS-like compounds also exhibited negative correlations with the relative
abundances of specific dominant pathogens (Fig. 3h). Notably, these negative associations
between biosynthetic gene clusters and pathogen abundance were consistent across both total
dominant pathogens and individual dominant pathogen taxa (Fig. 3h). Together, these findings
provide insights into specific microbial taxa and biosynthetic gene clusters associated with the
secondary metabolite biosynthetic capacity of pathogen-suppressive soils at a global scale,
highlighting their potential as candidate microbial features or putative indicators of reduced
pathogen prevalence.

Expansion risk of bacterial pathogens under climate change
Having identified current pathogen hotspots and the ecological drivers associated with soil
pathogen suppression, we next projected the distributions of dominant bacterial plant pathogens
under global change scenarios. By integrating key environmental predictors, we generated
predictive maps of both current and future distributions across global soils, explaining 64–77% of
the spatial variation in pathogen prevalence (Supplementary Table 2). Our analysis indicated a
notable prevalence of pathogens in areas with high temperatures, particularly in northern regions
of South America, North Africa, and South Asia (Fig. 4a). Future climate projections, especially
under global warming scenarios, suggest not only increased relative abundance in these areas but
also the emergence of new hotspots in northern Asia (Fig. 4b). This projected expansion mirrors
the predicted trends for fungal plant pathogens, which are similarly expected to intensify under
global change scenarios6. Streptomyces europaeiscabiei, a species predominant in arid regions, is
currently distributed across all continents, with higher relative abundance in Africa, Australia,
southwestern region of North America, and the southwestern part of Asia (Fig. 4c). Predictive
models forecast a future expansion of S. europaeiscabiei into northern Asia (Fig. 4d), suggesting
both range shifts and increases in dominance. Similarly, Ralstonia solanacearum, which thrives in
humid conditions, currently dominates equatorial regions including South Asia, northern South
America, northern Australia, eastern North America, and Central Africa (Fig. 4e). Future
projections indicate an increased dominance of this pathogen near equatorial zones (Fig. 4f).
Importantly, and despite employing independent analytical approaches, the distribution patterns of
R. solanacearum from our models closely matched records from the EPPO Global Database
(https://gd.eppo.int/)27, supporting the robustness of our predictive framework. Overall, our
predictive maps indicate a further increase in dominant bacterial plant pathogens across much of
the globe under anticipated future climatic conditions (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Figure 5).
Together, these results provide insights into the current and future global distributions of bacterial
plant pathogens and establish a basis for future empirical validation at regional and local scales,
as well as for the development of monitoring and disease risk assessment frameworks under global
change.

Overall, our findings have important implications for future research and for the monitoring and
management of plant disease risks. Future work should assess how the global drivers of pathogen
prevalence and suppression identified here interact with local factors, such as land-use practices,
crop management (e.g., resistant varieties, crop rotation), and regional socio-economic
constraints—to shape disease outcomes. While this study focuses on pathogen dominance and
suppression, predicting pathogen virulence and disease severity associated with dominance
represents an important next research direction. Establishing locally relevant thresholds for
microbial diversity, the abundance of key microbial taxa such as non-pathogenic Streptomyces
spp., or the presence of specific biosynthetic gene clusters could also enable the development of
practical indicators of pathogen-suppressive soils. Such indicators would provide a valuable basis
for improved surveillance systems and for designing targeted interventions, including microbial
inoculants or metabolite-based approaches, to mitigate disease risks in both agricultural and natural
ecosystems.

We present the comprehensive catalogue of globally dominant soil-borne bacterial plant pathogens
and provide insights into the environmental and biological factors associated with pathogen natural
suppression. Our results show that high soil microbial diversity, increased soil organic carbon, and
colder climates consistently coincide with lower pathogen prevalence worldwide. We also identify
specific microbial groups, including non-pathogenic Streptomyces spp., arbuscular mycorrhizal
fungi, and lichenized fungi, and biosynthetic gene clusters encoding terpenes and polyketides as
potential indicators of pathogen-suppressive soils. Our analyses indicate that several dominant
bacterial pathogens are likely to expand or increase in prevalence under future climate scenarios,
highlighting regions where disease risks may intensify. These findings advance our understanding
of the ecological processes shaping pathogen distributions and provide a foundation for developing
improved surveillance tools, management practices, and future research aimed at mitigating the
impacts of soil-borne bacterial diseases on global food production and ecosystem functioning.

## Methods

Global soil metagenomics (shotgun sequencing based) database
We developed global soil metagenomics database by combining metagenomes obtained from
public databases (including 1,402 metagenomes) and a standardized global soil sampling
(including 200 metagenomes). The public databases including the published global standardized
soil metagenome dataset, and soil metagenomes from global regions available from the NCBI SRA
database62,63. For the standardized global soil samples, topsoil (~0–10 cm) samples were collected
from a global soil survey conducted between 2016 and 2019, employing standardized field
protocols for all sampling procedures16. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was conducted at the
Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) Facility (Western Sydney University, Australia) using the
Illumina NovaSeq platform to generate approximately 10 Gb of 150 bp paired-end high-quality
reads per sample. In total, the combined database comprises soil metagenomes derived from 317
independent NCBI BioProjects, spanning data release years from 2011 to 2024 (Supplementary
Data 1).

Our final global dataset comprises 1,602 soil metagenomes collected from 23 terrestrial biomes
spanning 59 countries across all continents (Supplementary Figure 1). This dataset covers a broad
range of climate (arid, temperate, tropical, cold, and polar), and major vegetation types, including
grasslands, shrublands, forests, wetlands, and farmlands. We included soils from both agricultural
and natural ecosystems because natural soils provide an essential ecological baseline, can act as
reservoirs of pathogen inoculum, and offer an optimal context for examining natural pathogen
suppression, an ecological process that is often obscured by intensive management in agricultural
systems. Sampling locations were selected to capture a robust representation of Earth's
geographical, climatic and edaphic diversity, and all sites corresponded to natural or agricultural
soils rather than controlled experimental samples. For example, the latitude of the sampling
locations ranges from –77.6 to 80.7; the longitude ranges from –159.6 to 172.2, and plant cover
ranges between 0.1% and 100%. The mean annual temperature (MAT) varies between –24.8 and
27.8 ℃; the mean annual precipitation (MAP) ranges from 6 to 5895 mm, and the soil pH ranges
from 3.7 to 9.11. This broad coverage improves the representativeness of the dataset, enabling a
more comprehensive understanding of how environmental factors shape the global distribution of
soil plant bacterial pathogens.

Metagenomic analysis and potential bacterial plant pathogens detection
The global soil metagenomics database (1,602 samples) was used for the detection of potential
bacterial plant pathogens. Metagenomic tools like Kraken 245,64, MetaPhlAn265, and MG-RAST66,
enable high-resolution identification of microbial taxonomic information. However, these tools
are generally not tailored for the specific detection of bacterial plant pathogens. To enhance the
accuracy in identifying bacterial plant pathogens in soil samples, we developed a specialized, high-
quality database focused on bacterial plant pathogens (BPPDB). Guided by previous literature,
this database comprises 113 recognized bacterial plant pathogen species represented by 310
complete genomes obtained from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). By
capturing the majority of globally important bacterial plant pathogens, those responsible for a
substantial proportion of plant disease worldwide, BPPDB provides a biologically meaningful and
robust framework for large-scale pathogen identification, while maintaining an appropriate
balance between taxonomic coverage and genomic quality. The nucleotide sequences of these
pathogen genomes were then translated into protein sequences, followed by the construction of a
protein database using the DIAMOND67.

For the analysis of 1,602 shotgun metagenomic datasets, we first quality-filtered the raw sequences
using fastp (v0.20.1)68. The obtained high-quality reads were then assembled using Megahit
(v1.2.9)69, retaining contigs ≥1000 bp in length. We next used Prokka (v1.14.5)70 for gene
prediction to identify the open reading frames (ORFs, i.e., protein-coding genes). These ORFs
were then clustered at a 95% similarity threshold using CD-HIT (v4.8.1)71, to generate a non-
redundant gene catalogue. The read counts and Reads Per Million (RPM) values for each predicted
non-redundant gene were quantified using Salmon (v1.6.0)72. Subsequently, for the taxonomic
annotation of bacterial plant pathogens, we conducted an alignment of the translated protein
sequences from our soil metagenomic datasets against our customized bacterial plant pathogens
database using DIAMOND. This alignment was conducted under specific parameters: a maximum
e-value threshold of 1 × 10−10, a minimum percent identity of over 80%, and baseline alignment
length of at least 100 amino acids. The relative abundances of these bacterial phylotypes were
expressed as RPM across all samples, allowing direct comparison of relative abundance among
samples with differing sequencing depths and read yields73. In total, we identified 107 bacterial
pathogen species, of which 32 were classified as globally dominant based on their high frequency
of occurrence (present in at least 80% of samples) and high relative abundance (top 30%, with a
mean relative abundance ≥ 0.1%) across global soils (Fig. 1).

Cross-validation of pathogen detection
Comparison with Kraken 2 databases. We used a combination of Kraken 2 (v2.1.1)45 and Bracken
(v2.6.2)74 tools based on the standard Kraken database (as of March 2023) for the taxonomic
annotation at the reads level. We discerned 98 bacterial phylotypes overlapped with our custom
plant pathogenic bacterial database, from a total of 10,014 bacterial phylotypes detected. The
identified table was rarefied to 100,000 reads per sample for alpha-diversity estimation and
normalized using the cumulative sum scaling (CSS) method for beta-diversity analyses. Our results
indicated a significant and positive correlation between the alpha and beta diversity of bacterial
plant pathogens identified from our custom database workflow and those identified from the
Kraken 2 database (alpha diversity: r = 0.25, P < 2.2 × 10 −16; Beta diversity: r = 0.39, P < 2.2 ×
10 −16) (Supplementary Figure 6a & b). Furthermore, the relative abundances of most pathogens
identified from our database showed significantly positive correlation with those identified by
Kraken 2 database (Selected 15 pathogens, Pearson r 0.25–0.67, P < 2.2e-16; Supplementary
Figure 7).

Comparison with the PHI-base. We mapped aligned translated protein sequences from soil
metagenomic datasets to the validated virulence genes curated in the Pathogen-Host Interactions
database (PHI-base)75 utilizing the DIAMOND67 tool (e-value threshold of 1 × 10−10, percent
identity > 80%). This method effectively identified a significant count of 2250 functional genes
associated with bacterial pathogenicity and virulence. There are 23 annotated bacterial plant
pathogen species overlapped between the PHI-base and our custom database. Among them, the
relative abundance of most overlapping species showed a significant positive correlation between
two methods. In the analysis of individual species correlations, the top 12 most positively
correlated species exhibited Pearson r values ranging from 0.14 to 0.80, with P-values ranging
from < 6.591e-09 to < 2.2e-16 (Supplementary Figure 8).

Comparison with coverM quantification. We further performed an independent validation using
an alternative read-alignment–based method, CoverM76, to assess the robustness of our pathogen
abundance quantification. Estimates derived from Salmon and CoverM were highly consistent
(Pearson r = 0.95, P < 2.2e-16 for total pathogen abundance), with many individual pathogens
showing correlations exceeding 0.90 (P < 2.2e-16, Supplementary Figure 9).

Comparison with expanded pathogen database. To address the potential overestimation arising
from closely related non-pathogenic taxa, we expanded the bacterial plant pathogen database
(BPPDB) to include 20 genomes from closely related non-pathogenic species. Pathogen
abundances estimated derived from the expanded database were highly concordant with those
obtained using the pathogen-only database (Supplementary Figure 10, Pearson r > 0.98, P < 2.2e-
16).

Comparison with quantitative PCR of specific dominant pathogens. From the standardised
dataset, we retrieved DNA and performed pathogen-targeted qPCR assays to further validate the
abundances of bacterial plant pathogens identified using our custom database. Specifically, the
absolute abundance of Ralstonia solanacearum, the dominant plant pathogen identified in our data,
was quantified via real-time qPCR employing the primers FliCF
(GAACGCCAACGGTGCGAACT) and FliCR (GGCRGGCCTTCAGGGAGGTC)77. For these
assays, we randomly selected 70 samples spanning a range of biomes. The qPCR reactions were
assembled in a total volume of 10 μl, comprising 1 μ l of DNA template, 5 μl of 2×PowerUp SYBR
Green Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 3.2 μl of PCR-grade water, and 0.4 μl of both the
forward and reverse primers (10 μmol μl−1 each). The assays were carried out on a LightCycler
480 (Roche) utilizing a 3-step melt cure program on a LightCycler 480 (Roche), under the
following parameters: an initial denaturation at 95°C for 5 minutes, succeeded by 40 cycles of
denaturation at 95°C for 30 s, annealing at 60°C for 45 s, and elongation at 72°C for 60 s.
Following qPCR, amplification specificity was assessed through melting curve analysis, with
samples showing specific amplification retained for further analysis. The R. solanacearum isolate,
purchased from the Department of Primary Industries (DPI, NSW), provided the genomic DNA
for establishing standards in the qPCR assays. Standard curves were constructed using a tenfold
serial dilution. The comparison between the abundance of R.solanacearum from our custom
database and the absolute abundance from qPCR revealed a significant positive correlation (rho =
0.28, P = 0.018; Supplementary Figure 6c), demonstrating a strong concordance in the detection
and quantification of this pathogen.

Taxonomic microbial diversity and qPCR-based abundance
Soil microbial diversity was assessed using both metagenomic and amplicon sequencing data, with
amplicon sequencing conducted only for the 200 standardized global soil samples. For the 1,602
metagenomic samples, taxonomic profiles were generated using the Kraken 2 database. The
standardized dataset comprising the 200 global soil samples included both shotgun amplicon
sequencing data generated on the Illumina MiSeq platform, consisting of 16S rRNA gene and ITS
amplicon datasets (n = 200 each, 400 datasets in total). Bacterial and fungal communities were
characterized by amplifying the 16S rRNA and 18S rRNA genes using the 341F/805R and
Euk1391f/EukBr primer sets, respectively78,79. Samples were sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq
platform (2 × 300 PE) at the Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) Facility (Western Sydney
University, Australia) using a paired-end sequencing protocol. The microbial diversity of these
200 amplicon sequencing data was characterized using QIIME (v1.9.1)80, USEARCH (v10.0)81,
and UNOISE382. Amplicon Sequencing Variants (ASVs) were identified at the 100% identity level.
Representative sequences of bacterial ASVs were annotated against the SILVA database83, and
fungal ASVs were classified using both SILVA and the Protist Ribosomal Reference (PR2)
databases84. ASVs that could not be confidently assigned to bacterial or fungal lineages were
excluded from downstream analyses. The remaining reads were subsequently clustered into 37,653
bacterial and 6,083 fungal ASVs. For alpha-diversity estimation, the bacterial and fungal ASV
tables were rarefied to 10,000 sequences per sample (resulting in the removal of one sample) and
4,000 sequences per sample (removing 25 samples), respectively, as supported by the rarefaction
curves shown in Supplementary Figure 12. Despite the inherent limitations of short-read 18S data,
the fungal dataset provides reliable comparative diversity patterns suitable for large-scale cross-
biome analyses85. Microbial alpha-diversity was calculated in QIIME.

We also carried out 16S qPCR experiment for the 200 standardised global dataset to measure the
bacterial abundance in soil, using the primer set Eub338/Eub51886,87. The qPCR reactions were
assembled in a total volume of 10 μl, comprising 1 μl of DNA template, 5 μl of 2×PowerUp SYBR
Green Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 3.2 μl of PCR-grade water, and 0.4 μl of both the
forward and reverse primers (10 μmol μl−1 each). The assays were carried out on a LightCycler
480 (Roche) utilizing a 3-step melt cure program, using a 3-step melt cure program on a
LightCycler 480 (Roche), under the following parameters: an initial denaturation at 95°C for 5
minutes, succeeded by 45 cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 30 s, annealing at 57°C for 30 s, and
elongation at 72°C for 30 s. Standards were generated by cloning target sequences from pure
cultures into pUC57-Amp vector and weIre then transformed into chemically competent
Escherichia coli cells. Standard curves were generated using a tenfold serial dilution of plasmid
DNA.

Greenhouse experimental validation of soil microbial diversity-pathogen abundance
relationships
To validate the observed correlation between soil microbial diversity and pathogen abundance, a
controlled greenhouse experiment was conducted. Soil samples were collected from the
Hawkesbury Forest Experiment (HFE) site at the Hawkesbury Institute for the Environment (HIE),
Western Sydney University in December 2023. The soils were homogenized and sieved (2 mm
mesh) prior to experimental setup. A portion of the soil was temporarily stored at room temperature
(~25 ̊ C) and maintained at a 70% water-holding capacity moisture level for soil inoculation
preparation. The other portion of the soil was sterilized by > 50 kGy γ radiation with a 60Co source.
Soil microcosms were established using dilution-to-extinction approach47. An initial soil inoculum
(100-fold diluted inoculum) was prepared by mixing 20g unsterilized soil with 100 mL sterilized
demineralized water using a blender for 2 min. Four microbial diversity gradients including
sterilized soils, 10-6 diluted soils (by adding 150 mL106-fold diluted inoculums to 1.5 kg soil), 10-
3 diluted soils (by adding 150 mL 103-fold diluted inoculum to 1.5 kg soil), and natural soil. The
inoculated soils were incubated at room temperature for six months to facilitate microbial
community assembly and stabilization.

The representative pathogen strains S. scabiei and R. solanacearum were obtained from the New
South Wales Department of Primary Industries (DPI, Australia), originally isolated from diseased
potato and tomato plants, respectively. Bacterial cultures were grown in nutrient broth medium
under constant agitation (180 rpm) for 72 hr at 28°C. Cell densities were normalized to OD600 =
1.0 using sterilized water. Soil microcosms with defined microbial diversity gradients were
established in 3-L polyethylene pots containing 1.5 kg of sterilized soil. Following a 7-day pre-
incubation period with daily watering to 60% water-holding capacity, each microcosm was
inoculated with 15 mL bacterial suspension through soil drenching. Each treatment was replicated
five times. The applied inoculum corresponded to an estimated initial concentration of ~10⁶ CFU
per gram of soil, which lies within the commonly used range for soil-borne pathogen introduction
assays in controlled experiments88. All experimental units were maintained in controlled
greenhouse conditions (without host plants) with standardized irrigation protocols. Soil samples
were collected at 3 days, 14 days, and 21 days post-inoculation and immediately store at -20°C for
subsequent molecular analysis. At each time point, around 5 g of soil was collected from the top
0–5 cm layer using sterile corers, pooled from three subsites within the same pot to reduce spatial
heterogeneity. Soil was also sampled prior to pathogen inoculation to assess background pathogen
levels.

Total DNA was extracted from collected soil samples using the Powersoil DNA Isolation Kit (Mo
Bio Laboratories, Carlsbad, CA, USA), following the manufacturer’s instructions. The quality of
DNA was assessed using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, USA). The
absolute abundances of the inoculated pathogens were quantified by quantitative PCR (qPCR).
The absolute abundance of S. Scabiei was quantified using primers Stx1a
(GTGGACCGTGGAGCATCT) and Stx1b ( CAGTTCGGCGTAACTCAGC)89. For R.
solanacearum, primers FliCF (GAANCGCCAACGGTGCGAACT) and FliCR
(GGCGGCCTTCAGGGAGGTC)77 were used. Each qPCR reaction was performed in a total
volume of 10 μl, comprising 1 μl of DNA template, 5 μl of 2×PowerUp SYBR Green Master Mix
(Thermo Fisher Scientific), 3.2 μl of PCR-grade water, and 0.4 μl of both the forward and reverse
primers (10 μmol μl−1 each). The assays were carried out on a LightCycler 480 (Roche) utilizing
a 3-step melt cure program on a LightCycler 480 (Roche). For S. scabiei, the thermal profile
consisted of an initial denaturation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation at
95 °C for 15 s, annealing at 62 °C for 30 s, and extension at 72 °C for 45 s. For R. solanacearum, the
profile included an initial denaturation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation
at 95 °C for 30 s, annealing at 60 °C for 45 s, and extension at 72 °C for 60 s. Amplification
specificity was verified by melting curve analysis, and only samples showing specific
amplification were retained for further analysis.

Profiling functional genes of metagenomic data and pathogen genomes
For the metagenomic data, the functional genes of the ORFs were annotated using the eggNOG-
mapper v1.0.3, based on the eggNOG database (version 5.0)90. The annotation results were then
reorganized into Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) Orthology (KO)46 profiles.
Comparative genomic analysis was conducted to explore the genomic drivers determining the
distribution of pathogens. Initially, we categorized our pathogens into dominant and non-dominant
groups and compared the functional gene differences between these two groups. Differential
abundance analysis of functional genes between dominant and non-dominant pathogens was
performed using the generalized linear model (GLM) approach of EdgeR in the ‘edgeR’ R
package91, applying a trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) normalization method and a threshold
of significance set at P < 0.001. To identify microbial metabolic traits contributing to pathogen
suppression, we further annotated bacterial biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) in our metagenomic
dataset and examined their correlations with pathogen abundance. BGCs were predicted using
antiSMASH (v7.1)55 database on contigs larger than 3 kb. For precise product identification, the
predicted BGCs were aligned to those in the MIBiG92 repository using BLASTP.

Correlation between pathogen abundance and their known global distribution
We downloaded reported global distribution data of some bacterial plant pathogens from previous
studies and public databases to assess potential correlation between the distribution of bacterial
plant pathogens and their global distribution. We downloaded the data of the distribution of several
bacterial plant pathogens from the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization
(EPPO) Global Database (https://gd.eppo.int/)27. This data was then correlated with our data to
further elucidate the links between the abundance of these pathogens and their known global
distribution. We also extracted the global distribution data of R. solanacearum species complex
from a previous study26, and performed a correlation analysis with our dataset.

Environmental factors and soil properties measure
For both standardized global soil sampling and from public databases ((1,602 samples in total)),
climatic information, including mean annual temperature (MAT), mean annual precipitation
(MAP), diurnal temperature range (MDR), and seasonality of temperature (TSEA) and
precipitation (PSEA), was extracted from the WorldClim 2.0 database93 (1 km2 resolution). Aridity
index data were acquired from the Global Aridity Index and Potential Evapotranspiration Climate
Database (version 3)94. Assessment of plant cover (the fraction of ground covered by green
vegetation) were obtained from Copernicus Global Land Service95. The Normalized Difference
Vegetation Index (NDVI) were derived from Landsat 7 Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (ETM+)
imagery (with a pixel resolution of 30 m x 30 m), employing methods previously described96. In
the case of the global standardized dataset, soil properties were determined using standardized
protocols. Soil properties, such as pH, texture (quantified by clay percentage), salinity, total
organic nitrogen, and OC content were analysed using methodologies detailed in previous
studies96-98.

Evaluating the ecological drivers of bacterial plant pathogens
Machine learning random forest analyses were then performed using the ‘randomForest’99 and
‘rfPermute’ package100 in R to explore the ecological factors (such as MAT, MAP, NDVI, soil
properties, and microbial diversity) that drive the relative abundance of bacterial plant pathogens.
Each RF model was trained with 9,999 trees (ntree = 9999), using the default number of variables
randomly sampled at each split. A fixed random seed was used to ensure reproducibility. Variable
importance was quantified based on the Mean Decrease in Accuracy (%IncMSE) metric obtained
via the importance() function. The top-ranked predictors were exported for reproducibility.
Statistical significance of predictor importance was further assessed using rfPermute, which
applies permutation-based testing to derive p-values for each predictor’s contribution. All analyses
were repeated across 32 pathogen variables using a standardized workflow to ensure consistency
of variable importance ranking and model performance. Spearman correlation analyses were
further conducted to evaluate the correlations between ecological factors and the relative
abundance of all plant pathogens and the dominant plant pathogens using the R package ‘psych’101.
All statistical analyses were conducted and visualized in R (http://www.r-project.org).

Structural Equation Modeling (SEM)102 was further utilized to identify the direct and indirect
impacts of climatic factors, vegetation, soil properties, and microbial diversity on the relative
abundance of dominant bacterial plant pathogens. The SEM constructs were developed using IBM
SPSS Amos 21 software (Amos Development Corporation), following the methodology
established in previous studies6,52. Model estimation was performed using maximum likelihood.
Considering the non-normal distribution of some introduced variables, bootstrap tests were applied
to evaluate the probability of path coefficients differing from zero. Model fit was evaluated through
a chi-square test, the root mean squared error of approximation (RMSEA), and the Bollen–Stine
bootstrap test. Our models showed a robust fit, as indicated by the following metrics: chi-square/df
= 0.892, P = 0.345; RMSEA = 0.00, P = 0.821; and bootstrap P = 0.383.

Global mapping of bacterial plant pathogens
We next utilized ordinary least squares models to predict the current and future global distribution
of bacterial plant pathogens. Predictors for our global maps were selected through machine
learning using random forest regression, including climatic factors (MAP, MAT, MDR, and
PSEA), elevation, slope, vegetation (NDVI), and soil properties (organic carbon, texture, and pH).
Multicollinearity was assessed and used to filter predictors. To assess the accuracy of the models,
we quantified the discrepancy between the parameter space of the predictors and the original
dataset103. Areas in the projection distant from the sample points were pinpointed using a masking
criterion based on a P-value less than 0.01. We used the Mahalanobis distance to every point in
the multidimensional space, which spans across ten dimensions as determined by the exogenous
variables. This distance was measured in relation to both the center of the known distribution and
the convex hull encompassing all data points used in the model. Environmental outliers were
defined as locations whose Mahalanobis distance exceeded the 0.95 quantile of the χ² distribution
(df = 10), indicating that their environmental profiles did not fall within the multivariate envelope
of the sampled observations104.

To project the distribution of bacterial plant pathogens globally in future climates (2050), we reran
our original model, using climatic and land use available data sets following previous studies6,105-
108. The land-use projections were provided by the Land-use Harmonized v2.0 project
(http://luh.umd.edu/)109 whereas climatic variables were obtained from MIROC6 global climate
model (CMIP6 Landscape 2019)110. Key constant variables in these projections were elevation,
slope, and soil properties. We used a mix of historical and future datasets from ISMIP2a under
Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 2.6, RCP6.0, and RCP8.5 for the year 2050,
integrating these with Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP)105,111.

Map images in Figure 2c, 4a–f and Supplementary Figure 1, 5a–m were created in R using
ggplot2112.

### Reviewer 1

This study presents a global atlas of soil-borne pathogens using 1,602 soil metagenomes from over 50 countries. They used amplicon sequencing, qPCR, greenhouse validation experiments, and performed predictive modeling for climate change scenarios. This is a timely study that provides interesting insights. For example, how pathogen suppression may be negatively linked to mycorrhizal fungi, non-pathogenic Streptomyces, organic carbon, and some of the biosynthetic gene clusters. I also appreciate their attempts to predict things under climate change. However, there are several methodological, and conceptual issues that must be addressed before the manuscript can be considered further.
Introduction
Ln 93-94: But why? What are the current challenges that prevent such studies?
Ln 96-98: that’s not completely right. Check out this study (doi:10.1016/j.oneear.2024.06.005) that found that high microbial diversity prevents pathogen prevalence worldwide.
Ln 115-117: I believe the authors can be more specific and directional in their hypothesis. It’s a bit vague at the moment. A lot of factors will jointly either promote or suppress sounds too ambiguous.
Methods
Database assembly: this section is confusing as the authors discuss amplicon data and metagenome data simultaneously. I suggest separating the two types of data. However, I do have some other questions. Did you only select field samples or you also selected greenhouse samples? I ask because while both would show a location on global map, they are completely different. Plant pathogen studies are often conducted in the greenhouse. Some of the land use sites also do not make sense. For example, wetland, forest, and bare land—what’s the rationale when you are interested in plant pathogens? Secondly, did you select studies that used same/ similar sequencing platforms and depths? Microbiome meta-analyses are always tricky because primer sets are different, instruments are different, terrible reverse reads, meta-data are not available most of the times, etc. How did you ensure/overcome this? Ln 755 says: “We used shotgun metagenomic data for the detection of potential bacterial plant pathogens”- which samples are these? Standardized or global? Lastly, the custom dataset is a strength, but with 137 species and 310 genomes, it probably doesn’t represent the global diversity of plant pathogens. The authors used Salmon for quantification. While it’s a widely used tool, there are inherent biases with regards to its correction assumptions and how it handles similar isoforms. The protein-level homology cut-off used in this study can overestimate the detection of pathogens by including non-pathogenic close relatives. This also becomes a problem since the correlations for the top 12 most positively correlated species were as low as 0.14.
Fungal data: The Euk primers are good for a lot of eukaryotic organisms, so it seems like one stone for many birds. However, for fungi, it provides very poor resolution and this becomes an even bigger problem since the typical amplicon size derived from these primers is really short (~180 bp). Furthermore, the threshold for rarefying fungal data is also too low. I feel the fungal dataset is suboptimal. These caveats should be mentioned explicitly and rarefaction plots should be provided for both bacteria and fungi.
Greenhouse study: I appreciate that the authors attempted to validate their diversity-pathogen relationship, but there are important issues. First of all, it is not clear if this greenhouse study was conducted in the presence of a host plant or not. If not, why do it in the greenhouse? Secondly, the authors used OD600 and inoculated a 15 mL suspension. OD600 is a crude measure and can be affected by dead cells and different sizes, especially in this case. Cell count using Flow Cytometry would have been better. More importantly, 15 mL reads arbitrary- why 15 and not 10 or 20? Was it adequate for a 3 L pot? Did you just add it on top of the pots or a few mm into the soil? When you collected samples, did you collect from the topsoil, especially since the pot size was 3 L. Also, how much soil sample was collected at each time point? Important details are missing. Lastly, the validation only involved two pathogens- Streptomyces scabiei and Ralstonia solanacearum, so the findings must be interpreted with caution.
Statistics: Provide important details on RF, SEM and network analysis? P values, correlation thresholds, etc.? Ln 968: how did you identify outliers and how many were they?
Results and Discussion
Dominant pathogen: I find their threshold for defining a dominant pathogen too stringent. Prevalence of 100% of samples and relative abundance in the top 30% can bias the dataset towards only ubiquity and ignore locally devastating pathogens. Basically, relative abundance and presence (ubiquity) do not necessarily correspond to virulence potential.
The relationship between microbial diversity and pathogen is not really strong. Sometimes it was even less than 0.01. I wouldn’t call it ‘robust’. Exercise caution while interpreting.
While climatic factors are certainly important for pathogen prevalence, as shown in this study, management and agronomic factors are also critical. For example, the application of fungicides or pesticides, adoption of resistant varieties and crop rotation, etc. can determine pathogen outbreaks and prevalence at a local scale, potentially impacting global scale projections done in this study. I would be careful in interpretations and conclusions and not attribute everything to climate change.
Figures 1 and 3 are just too dense. Too much to process in my opinion.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript entitled “Dominance and natural suppression of bacterial plant pathogens across global soils” by Gao et al., identified 32 dominant bacterial plant pathogens, their genomic traits, and evidence of natural soil suppression, by combining a global survey and public databases, including 1,602 soil metagenomes and an independent greenhouse experiment. The authors found that pathogen suppression was strongest in global cold-climate hot-spots, driven by high soil organic carbon, microbial diversity, and abundance; non-pathogenic Streptomyces, mycorrhizal fungi, lichenized fungi, and terpene/polyketide gene clusters all negatively correlated with pathogen prevalence; and that future climates are projected to increase many pathogens, particularly in tropical Africa, North America, and Eurasia. This study establishes a foundational atlas of soil-borne plant pathogens, advancing ecological knowledge and guiding future surveillance and management to protect food security and sustainability. Overall, the research topic is very interesting and important, but I have several critical comments.
Major comments:
1. The dilution-to-extinction approach presents a potential confounding factor, as it might inadvertently introduce bacterial pathogens. The manuscript should address the extent of this potential influence. Furthermore, the experimental design requires clarification regarding the controls used—for instance, whether a set of dilutions was maintained without pathogen inoculation to account for background effects. Additionally, it is crucial to justify whether the chosen sampling period (3 to 21 days post-inoculation) was sufficient for the microbial community to stabilize.
2. The authors found that bacterial and fungal diversity were very important for pathogen suppression, but the description of bacterial and fungal sequencing protocols lacks sufficient detail. I think the authors should be more detailed in bacterial and fungal sequence. After resampling, each fungal sample had 2,000 sequences. Does this sequence depth adequately capture the diversity of the entire fungal community? I recommend including a rarefaction curve to address this concern. Additionally, the authors should expand their Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to include microbial metabolic traits. The current model, which focuses on diversity, is incomplete given the documented crucial role of metabolic traits in pathogen suppression.
3. The Methods section lacks sufficient detail. Although Random Forest models and were employed, their implementation is not described. The manuscript must clarify the cross-validation procedure, the specific parameters used, and the performance metrics (e.g., whether the F1-score was applied). I suggest consulting the documentation for relevant packages (e.g., rfPermute or A3) to ensure these crucial details are explicitly reported.
4. The manuscript would benefit from stylistic refinement to enhance its overall clarity and fluency. Numerous sentences are structurally unwieldy and hinder readability. For instance, the sentence in Lines 324-327 is characteristic of this issue, as it relies heavily on repetitive verbs such as “provide” and “offer”. A more concise and dynamic revision would significantly improve the impact. Additionally, I think grammar across the main text should be carefully re-checked by authors, since I found many grammar mistakes.
Some other minor comments:

2. Lines 69-72: This sentence is vague. Please clarify.
3. Line 89: Replace “e.g.” with “e.g.,”.
4. Line 108: Is “soil microbial biodiversity”?
5. Lines 132-133: Throughout the manuscript, italics should be used for all formally recognized taxonomic genera and species, such as Streptomyces, Rhodococcus, and Agrobacterium.

8. Line 226-232: The dilution-to-extinction approach could also introduce bacterial pathogens, and if so, to what extent?
Furthermore, what is the design of the control for this experiment (e.g., without inoculating the pathogen at each dilution gradient)?
9. Why is the natural soil treatment for Ralstonia solanacearum missing from Figure 3? I think the authors should add it.
10. Why only bacterial abundance? I suggest the authors should also investigate the relationship between fungal abundance and bacterial plant pathogens.
11. Line 235 and 240: If fungal abundance was not assessed, I suggest replacing “abundances” and with “bacterial abundances”.
